lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: Alluvial gold mining is the recovery of gold from sand, gravel, and soil that has been eroded from primary rock deposits and transported by water. In Africa, this is the most common form of artisanal mining because it requires less capital and technical skill than hard rock mining. Rivers like the Offin in Ghana, the Niger in Mali, and the Zambezi in Zimbabwe have supported alluvial mining for centuries. Gold particles are heavy (specific gravity 19.3) and settle in river bends, behind boulders, and in gravel layers. You can find fine flakes, small nuggets, or dust. The key is to find where the river slows down and drops its heavy load. This module teaches you how to locate, extract, and process alluvial gold safely and efficiently. You will learn to read a river, use simple tools like pans, sluices, and shovels, and avoid common mistakes that lose gold. Alluvial mining can be done by one person or a small team. It is low-cost but requires patience and observation. In many African countries, alluvial mining is legal with a permit, but you must respect environmental rules and community water rights. This module will give you the practical skills to start, but always check local laws. Remember: gold is where you find it, but you must know where to look.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To mine alluvial gold, you need a few basic tools that are affordable and available in most African markets. The most important is a gold pan. A 14-inch plastic or metal pan with riffles works well. You can buy one for about $10-15, or make one from a car tire inner tube cut into a shallow bowl. Next, a shovel and a pickaxe for digging gravel. A bucket or two for carrying material. A sluice box is a game-changer for processing more gravel. You can build one from wood or buy a small one for $50-100. It uses a series of riffles and a water flow to catch gold. You also need a classifier or sieve to remove large rocks. A 1/2-inch mesh screen is ideal. For safety, bring gloves, boots, and a first-aid kit. A small vial or film canister for storing your gold. A magnet is useful to remove black sand (magnetite) from your concentrate. For river mining, you may need a small pump or just use the river current. A crevice tool or spoon helps clean cracks in bedrock. Always carry drinking water and food. In Africa, many miners use a 'batea' (wooden bowl) or a 'kuru' (calabash) as a pan. These are cheap and effective. Don't forget a headlamp if working at dawn or dusk. Keep your tools clean and in good repair. A broken shovel or torn sluice mat costs you gold. Finally, a notebook to record where you find gold and how much. This helps you return to good spots.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Step 1: Find a good spot. Look for inside bends of rivers, behind large rocks, and where the river widens and slows. Gold settles in these low-energy zones. Also check gravel bars and exposed bedrock. Step 2: Test panning. Take a panful of gravel from different spots. Pan it down to see if there is gold. If you see colors (fine gold), dig there. Step 3: Dig and classify. Use your shovel to dig gravel from the pay streak, which is usually a layer of gravel on bedrock or clay. Put it through your classifier to remove rocks larger than 1/2 inch. Step 4: Pan or sluice. If using a pan, fill it half with gravel, add water, and swirl. Remove large stones, then tilt and shake to let gold settle. Repeat until only black sand and gold remain. If using a sluice, set it in the river with a gentle slope. Feed classified gravel slowly. The riffles catch gold. Step 5: Clean up. Every few hours, clean the sluice by removing the mat and washing it into a bucket. Pan the concentrate to get your gold. Step 6: Store your gold. Dry it and put it in a vial. Weigh it if you have a scale. Step 7: Reclaim the site. Fill your holes and don't leave mercury or trash. In Africa, many miners work in teams: one digs, one carries, one pans. This is efficient. Work upstream to downstream. Always check your tailings (waste) for gold you might have missed. A common method is to use a 'long tom' or 'sluice box' with a gentle flow. Remember: slow and steady wins. Rushing loses gold.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Mistake 1: Panning too fast. If you swirl too quickly, gold washes out. Fix: Use a gentle circular motion and let the gold settle. Mistake 2: Not classifying. Large rocks hide gold and make panning hard. Fix: Always screen your gravel to 1/2 inch or smaller. Mistake 3: Using too much water flow in a sluice. Fast water flushes gold out. Fix: Adjust the slope and water speed so the flow is just enough to move gravel, not gold. Mistake 4: Digging in the wrong place. Many miners dig anywhere. Fix: Test pan first. Gold is patchy. Find the pay streak. Mistake 5: Losing fine gold. Fine gold floats or washes away. Fix: Use a sluice with fine riffles or a pan with deep riffles. Add a drop of dish soap to break surface tension. Mistake 6: Not checking tailings. You might be throwing away gold. Fix: Re-pan your tailings once a week. Mistake 7: Working alone in dangerous areas. Fix: Work in pairs or groups. Mistake 8: Ignoring safety. Fix: Wear gloves, boots, and don't work under overhanging banks. Mistake 9: Using mercury without retort. Mercury is toxic. Fix: Avoid mercury; use gravity methods. If you must, use a retort and never in water. Mistake 10: Not cleaning equipment. Fix: Clean your sluice and pan after each session. Gold sticks to dirt. Mistake 11: Giving up too soon. Fix: Gold mining requires persistence. Test many spots. In Africa, many miners fail because they don't test. A simple fix is to spend one day just panning test holes. That saves weeks of wasted digging.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Safety first. Alluvial mining can be dangerous. Rivers can rise quickly. Never work in a river during heavy rain or upstream of a dam. Always check weather. Work with a buddy. Wear boots with good grip, gloves, and a hat. Use sunscreen. Stay hydrated. If you dig in a bank, watch for collapse. Never undercut a bank. Keep your tools sharp and in good condition. A dull shovel causes accidents. If you use a sluice, set it on stable ground. Don't stand in fast water above your knees. If you use mercury, it is highly toxic. Inhaling vapors causes brain damage. Never use mercury near water or food. Use a retort and always in a ventilated area. Better yet, avoid mercury entirely. Gravity methods work fine for alluvial gold. Best practice: Fill your holes. Don't leave open pits. They are dangerous for people and animals. Don't cut trees unnecessarily. Respect local water sources. In many African communities, water is shared. Don't muddy the water downstream. Use settling ponds. Don't use chemicals like cyanide. It kills fish and people. If you find a large nugget, don't tell everyone. Theft is common. Store your gold securely. Work legally. Get a permit from the local mining authority. Pay taxes. This protects you. Finally, take breaks. Mining is hard work. Fatigue causes mistakes. Eat well. Sleep well. And always have a first-aid kit with bandages, antiseptic, and rehydration salts. In remote areas, know the nearest clinic. Safety is not optional. It is part of the job.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: Now it's time to practice. Find a local river or stream known for gold. If you don't have one, use a sandy area with a known gold history. You will need: a gold pan, shovel, bucket, classifier, and a vial. Step 1: Choose a test spot. Look for a gravel bar on the inside bend. Dig a hole 1 foot deep. Step 2: Take a panful of gravel from the bottom of the hole (on bedrock if possible). Step 3: Classify the gravel through your screen. Step 4: Pan it. Fill your pan with water, remove large rocks, then swirl gently. Tilt the pan and let the gold settle. Repeat until you see black sand. Look for gold colors. Step 5: Record your result. Did you find gold? How many flakes? Step 6: Move 10 feet upstream and repeat. Do this 5 times. Step 7: If you find gold, dig a larger hole and process more gravel. If not, move to another spot. Step 8: Practice using a sluice. Set it in the river at a slight angle. Feed classified gravel slowly. After 1 hour, clean the sluice and pan the concentrate. Step 9: Weigh your gold if you have a scale. Even 0.1 gram is a success. Step 10: Clean up. Fill your holes. Take your trash. For a team exercise, split into groups: diggers, carriers, panners. Time yourselves. See who finds the most gold in 2 hours. This builds skill and speed. Remember: the goal is to learn, not to get rich in one day. Repeat this exercise weekly. Keep a log of your best spots. In Africa, many successful miners started with just this simple test. Good luck!

quiz.q: What is alluvial gold?
options: A) Gold found in hard rock
B) Gold transported and deposited by water
C) Gold found in underground veins
D) Gold made by chemical processes
quiz.explanation: Alluvial gold is eroded from primary deposits and moved by water.

quiz.q: Which river in Ghana is known for alluvial gold?
quiz.explanation: The Offin River in Ghana has a long history of alluvial gold mining.

quiz.q: What is the specific gravity of gold?
quiz.explanation: Gold's high specific gravity (19.3) makes it settle in river bends.

quiz.q: Where does gold typically settle in a river?
options: B) Inside bends and behind rocks
quiz.explanation: Gold settles where water slows down, such as inside bends and behind obstacles.

quiz.q: What is the most important tool for alluvial mining?
quiz.explanation: A gold pan is essential for testing and processing small amounts of gravel.

quiz.q: What size mesh is recommended for a classifier?
quiz.explanation: A 1/2-inch screen removes large rocks while letting gold-bearing gravel through.

quiz.q: What is a sluice box used for?
quiz.explanation: A sluice box uses riffles and water flow to catch gold particles.

quiz.q: Why should you use a magnet in panning?
quiz.explanation: A magnet removes magnetite (black sand) from your concentrate.

quiz.q: What is a 'batea'?
options: B) A wooden bowl used for panning
quiz.explanation: A batea is a traditional wooden pan used in Africa and South America.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the step-by-step method?
quiz.explanation: Locating a promising spot is the first step before digging.

quiz.q: What is a 'pay streak'?
options: A) A layer of gold-bearing gravel
quiz.explanation: A pay streak is the layer of gravel on bedrock that contains gold.

quiz.q: Why should you classify gravel before panning?
options: A) To make panning easier and recover more gold
quiz.explanation: Classifying removes large rocks that hide gold and hinder panning.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when panning?
quiz.explanation: Panning too fast washes gold out of the pan.

quiz.q: How can you prevent fine gold from floating?
options: B) Add a drop of dish soap
quiz.explanation: Dish soap breaks surface tension so fine gold sinks.

quiz.q: What should you do with your tailings?
options: B) Re-pan them to check for missed gold
quiz.explanation: Tailings may still contain gold; re-panning recovers missed particles.

quiz.q: Why is mercury dangerous?
options: B) It is toxic and causes brain damage
quiz.explanation: Mercury vapor is highly toxic and can cause severe health problems.

quiz.q: What is a safe alternative to mercury for alluvial gold?
options: B) Gravity methods like panning and sluicing
quiz.explanation: Gravity methods are safe and effective for alluvial gold.

quiz.q: What should you do before working in a river?
options: A) Check weather and water level
quiz.explanation: Checking weather prevents being caught by flash floods.

quiz.q: Why should you fill your holes after mining?
options: B) To prevent accidents and respect the environment
quiz.explanation: Filling holes prevents injuries to people and animals.

quiz.q: What is a best practice for water use?
quiz.explanation: Settling ponds reduce pollution and respect other water users.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a large nugget?
options: B) Store it securely and quietly
quiz.explanation: Large nuggets attract theft; keep it secure.

quiz.q: Why is it important to get a mining permit?
options: B) It protects you legally and ensures taxes
D) It is only for large companies
quiz.explanation: A permit makes your operation legal and protects your rights.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the practical exercise?
options: B) To practice and learn skills
D) To find a mining partner
quiz.explanation: The exercise builds practical skills through repetition.

quiz.q: How many test holes should you dig in the exercise?
quiz.explanation: Digging 5 test holes helps you find a pay streak.

quiz.q: What should you record in your logbook?
options: B) Locations and amounts of gold found
quiz.explanation: Recording locations and results helps you return to good spots.

quiz.q: What is a 'long tom'?
quiz.explanation: A long tom is a type of sluice box used in alluvial mining.

quiz.q: Why should you work upstream to downstream?
options: A) To avoid muddying your own water
quiz.explanation: Working upstream prevents your own muddy water from disturbing your work.

quiz.q: What is the recommended slope for a sluice box?
options: B) Slight angle with gentle flow
C) Steep angle with fast flow
quiz.explanation: A slight angle with gentle flow allows gold to settle in riffles.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see black sand in your pan?
options: B) Look for gold among it
quiz.explanation: Black sand often accompanies gold; pan carefully to reveal gold.

quiz.q: What is the most important safety rule when mining near water?
quiz.explanation: Working with a buddy ensures help is available in an emergency.
